pathogen_scientific_name.quote: The primary pathogen that causes anthracnose in the Midwest is the fungus Colletotrichum truncatum

type_of_disease.quote: The primary pathogen that causes anthracnose in the Midwest is the fungus Colletotrichum truncatum

affected_parts.quote: brown, irregularly shaped spots on stem, pods and petioles. The girding of petioles by large lesions results in premature defoliation. When pods are infected, mycelium may completely fill the cavity and no seeds are produced (pod blanking) or fewer and/or smaller seed form. Seed that does form may appear brown, moldy and shriveled or may look normal. Leaf infections result in leaf rolling, necrosis of laminar veins, petiole cankers and premature defoliation.

summary.value: Brown, irregularly shaped spots on stems, pods and petioles; seedlings develop sunken, dark brown lesions on cotyledons that may expand to stems; dark acervuli (pin cushion-like structures) develop in lesions on all tissue areas. Infected leaves develop brown veins and curl up, and brown cankers can appear on petioles causing defoliation.
summary.quote: The most common symptoms are brown, irregularly shaped spots on stem, pods and petioles. Sunken, dark brown lesions develop on the cotyledons of seedlings. Seedling lesions may expand to the stem and kill young plants. Dark acervuli develop in lesions on all host tissue areas.

diagnostic_features.value: Dark bodies looking like 'pin cushions' (acervuli) on plant surface visible at 20X magnification or greater; tiny black spines (setae) visible with 10X hand lens on infected areas; brown irregularly shaped spots on stems, pods and petioles; pod blanking where mycelium completely fills pod cavity.
diagnostic_features.quote: The fungus produces crowded, black acervuli on infected tissues. This will be dark bodies looking much like "pin cushions" on the plant surface when viewed with 20X or greater magnification. When pods are infected, mycelium may completely fill the cavity and no seeds are produced (pod blanking)

look_alikes.quote: Although the symptoms of anthracnose can be mistaken for pod and stem blight, the symptoms are different and both diseases may be present on the same plants late in the season.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Pseudomonas syringae pv. glycinea is the causal agent of bacterial blight in soybean.

type_of_disease.quote: Pseudomonas syringae pv. glycinea is the causal agent of bacterial blight in soybean. This pathogen survives in crop residue and can be seed transmitted.

affected_parts.quote: Bacterial blight can occur on all above ground plant parts, but is most evident on leaves in the mid to upper canopy... Infection can also occur on stems, petioles, pods, and seeds in infected pods.

summary.value: Infections begin as small, angular, water-soaked spots that turn yellow and then brown as the tissue dies. Lesions have dark reddish-brown centers surrounded by yellowish-green halos around water-soaked tissue; lesions may coalesce to form large, irregularly shaped lesions. Leaf veins may become affected creating necrotic areas resembling lightning on the leaf. Eventually lesions fall out leaving ragged foliage.
summary.quote: Infections begin as small, angular, water-soaked spots that turn yellow and then brown as the tissue dies. The spots darken and are surrounded by yellowish-green halos.

diagnostic_features.value: Presence of a yellowish-green halo around lesions; most common on young leaves in mid to upper canopy whereas brown spot is usually seen on older, lower leaves; lack of fungal structures in lesions.
diagnostic_features.quote: The two diseases can be distinguished by the presence of a halo around bacterial blight lesions... bacterial blight is most common on young leaves whereas brown spot is usually seen on older, lower leaves in the plant.

look_alikes.quote: Bacterial blight can be mistaken for Septoria brown spot.

conflicts.note: CropWatch Nebraska lists the pathogen as Pseudomonas savastanoi, which is considered an outdated or alternative name. The accepted pathogen name used by NC State Extension and UMN Extension is Pseudomonas syringae pv. glycinea.
CropWatch Nebraska and NC State only mention foliar, pod, and seed; UMN Extension additionally lists stem and petioles as affected.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: BSR is caused by the soilborne fungus Phialophora gregata

type_of_disease.quote: BSR is caused by the soilborne fungus Phialophora gregata

affected_parts.quote: The most characteristic symptom of BSR is the brown discoloration of the pith especially at and between nodes near the soil line. Foliar symptoms include interveinal chlorosis and necrosis. P. gregata infects soybean roots early in the growing season. It then moves up into the stems, invading the vascular system

summary.value: Brown discoloration of the stem pith, especially at and between nodes near the soil line; foliar symptoms include interveinal chlorosis and necrosis (yellowing and browning of tissue between leaf veins), followed by leaf wilting and curling.
summary.quote: The most characteristic symptom of BSR is the brown discoloration of the pith especially at and between nodes near the soil line. Foliar symptoms include interveinal chlorosis and necrosis (i.e., yellowing and browning of tissue between leaf veins), followed by leaf wilting and curling.

diagnostic_features.value: Brown discoloration of the pith (internal stem tissue), best observed at full pod stage; the pith remains brown unlike in sudden death syndrome where it stays white or cream-colored.
diagnostic_features.quote: The most characteristic symptom of BSR is the brown discoloration of the pith especially at and between nodes near the soil line. This symptom is best scouted for at full pod stage. However, in the case of sudden death syndrome (SDS), the pith of affected soybean plants will remain white or cream-colored.

look_alikes.quote: Foliar symptoms of BSR can be confused with those of sudden death syndrome

conflicts.note: UMN Extension lists only Foliar and Stem; PDDC (UW-Madison) additionally notes Root and Vascular involvement based on pathogen movement
UMN Extension notes 'Phialophora gregata, also named Cadophora gregata'; Cadophora gregata is an alternate name used in some literature

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Bean pod mottle is caused by bean pod mottle virus (BPMV).

type_of_disease.quote: BPMV is a member of the genus Comovirus in the family Comoviridae. Morphologically the virus is comprised by a bipartite, positive, single-stranded RNA.

affected_parts.quote: Bean pod mottle virus causes green to yellow mottling of young leaves. In severe infections, leaves may become distorted. Seeds from infected plants may be mottled or discolored, but other factors can also cause mottled seed. Symptoms may not be apparent at high temperatures or after pod set. Pod formation may be reduced when infected plants are under moisture stress. BPMV may also be related to the development of green stem syndrome, in which plants retain green stems and leaves after pods and most nearby plants have matured.

summary.value: Symptoms range from mild chlorotic mottling of foliage to severe mosaic on younger leaves, with possible leaf distortion, stunting, puckering, and reduced pod size in severe infections. Seeds from infected plants may be mottled or discolored. Green stem syndrome may also occur.
summary.quote: Symptoms first appear on the younger leaves and can range from mild chlorotic mottling of foliage to a severe mosaic. Green stem may also occur. In severe infections, stunting, leaf distortion and puckering and reduced pod size are also common.

diagnostic_features.value: Symptom development favored by cool temperatures but may not be apparent at higher temperatures or after pod set. No physical signs of the pathogen are present; confirmation requires lab testing. BPMV may also cause green stem syndrome where plants retain green stems and leaves after pods and nearby plants have matured.
diagnostic_features.quote: Symptom development is favored by cool temperatures, but may not be apparent in higher temperatures or after pod set. Since BPMV is caused by a virus, there are no physical signs of the pathgogen and the presence of the disease in the field needs to be confirmed through lab testing.

look_alikes.quote: BPMV can interact with the soybean mosaic virus to create severe symptoms in plants infected by both viruses.

conflicts.note: NC State Extension does not explicitly mention seed discoloration; UMN Extension mentions mottled or discolored seeds from infected plants.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Cercospora kikuchii is the causal pathogen of Cercospora leaf blight and purple seed stain in soybean

type_of_disease.quote: The asexual stage of this fungus is important for disease in soybean

affected_parts.quote: Reddish-purple lesions may also occur on petioles, stems, and pods. Infected seeds have pink to purple discoloration on the seed coats.

summary.value: The first symptom is the development of light purple spots and areas on the top surface of leaves exposed to light. The discolored areas expand and deepen in color to a reddish-purple or bronze. The infected leaves appear leathery and 'sunburned'. Red-brown spots may develop on both leaf surfaces and may coalesce to form large necrotic areas, eventually resulting in defoliation of infected leaves in the upper canopy.
summary.quote: The first symptom of Cercospora leaf blight is the development of light purple spots and areas on the top surface of leaves exposed to light. The discolored areas expand and deepen in color to a reddish-purple or bronze. The infected leaves appear leathery and 'sunburned'. Red-brown spots may develop on both leaf surfaces. The spots may coalesce to form large necrotic areas on leaves, which eventually results in defoliation of infected leaves in the upper canopy.

diagnostic_features.value: Purple-bronze discoloration on leaf surface caused by cercosporin toxin produced in the presence of light; small dark spots along major leaf veins and petioles; leaves wrinkle and become tough as disease progresses. Reddish-purple lesions on petioles, stems, and pods; pink to purple discoloration on seed coats.
diagnostic_features.quote: In the presence of light, the pathogen produces a toxin called cercosporin, which is responsible for the purple-bronze discoloration on the leaf surface... As the disease progresses small, dark spots will appear along major leaf veins and petioles and eventually the leaf will wrinkle and become tough.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Cercospora kikuchii is the causal pathogen of Cercospora leaf blight and purple seed stain in soybean

type_of_disease.quote: The asexual stage of this fungus is important for disease in soybean

affected_parts.quote: Soybean pods can also be infected by C. kikuchii, causing a disease called purple seed stain

summary.value: Pink to purple discoloration on seed coats of infected seeds; soybean pods infected by C. kikuchii develop purple seed stain.
summary.quote: Infected seeds have pink to purple discoloration on the seed coats.

diagnostic_features.value: Pink to purple discoloration specifically on seed coats
diagnostic_features.quote: Infected seeds have pink to purple discoloration on the seed coats.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Bacterial pustule is caused by the bacterium Xanthomonas axonopodis pv. glycines

type_of_disease.quote: Bacterial pustule is caused by the bacterium Xanthomonas axonopodis pv. glycines

affected_parts.quote: Symptoms begin as small, light green spots (not water-soaked) with raised centers on the upper and lower surfaces of leaves. Light-colored pustules (blisters) often develop in the center of lesions, especially on the undersides of leaves. [...] Small raised spots may also develop on pods.

summary.value: Small, light green spots with raised centers on leaf surfaces that develop into light-colored pustules (blisters), especially on undersides of leaves. Lesions can grow together into large irregular brown areas, and small raised spots may also develop on pods.
summary.quote: Symptoms begin as small, light green spots (not water-soaked) with raised centers on the upper and lower surfaces of leaves. Light-colored pustules (blisters) often develop in the center of lesions, especially on the undersides of leaves. The lesions can grow together into large irregular brown areas. [...] Small raised spots may also develop on pods.

diagnostic_features.value: Lack of water soaking at initial infection site, less chlorosis around lesions, tiny tan bumps on undersides of leaves without openings or spore masses (unlike soybean rust pustules). If an opening is present on the pustule, it is typically a linear crack across the surface.
diagnostic_features.quote: Bacterial pustule can be differentiated by a lack of water soaking at the initial site of infection, less chlorosis around lesions, and by the formation of tiny tan bumps on the undersides of leaves. The pustules can be mistaken for those of soybean rust, however, bacterial pustule does not have an opening in the pustules or masses of spores like those of soybean rust.

look_alikes.quote: Early symptoms of bacterial pustule look similar to bacterial blight. [...] The pustules can be mistaken for those of soybean rust, however, bacterial pustule does not have an opening in the pustules or masses of spores like those of soybean rust.

conflicts.note: OSU and CropWatch Nebraska only list foliar symptoms; UMN Extension also notes small raised spots on pods.
OSU source lists Xanthomonas axonopodis (syn. campestris) pv glycines, noting the synonym; canonical name follows UMN and CropWatch Nebraska usage.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Charcoal rot is caused by the soilborne fungus Macrophomina phaseolina

type_of_disease.quote: Charcoal rot is caused by the soilborne fungus Macrophomina phaseolina

affected_parts.quote: At the seedling stage, typical symptoms include , brown to dark spots on cotyledons. At the unifoliate leaf stage (VC), circular to oblong, reddish-brown, lesions that eventually turn dark brown to black may be observed. Mid to late season aboveground symptoms include light brown to grey superficial lesions in the stem. A characteristic sign of the pathogen on soybean is the presence of microsclerotia in the vascular tissue, in the pith, and mature and dry pods. Cross-sections of the lower stem and taproot may become streaked with gray hyphae and microsclerotia

summary.value: Brown to dark spots on cotyledons at seedling stage; circular to oblong reddish-brown to black lesions at unifoliate stage; light brown to grey superficial stem lesions mid to late season; roots and stems near soil surface appear gray with tiny black specks or dots resembling charcoal dust; cross-sections of lower stem and taproot streaked with gray hyphae and microsclerotia giving a marbled appearance; reddish-brown discoloration in pith and vascular tissues; plants may be stunted and wilted with small chlorotic and necrotic leaves that remain attached.
summary.quote: At the seedling stage, typical symptoms include , brown to dark spots on cotyledons. At the unifoliate leaf stage (VC), circular to oblong, reddish-brown, lesions that eventually turn dark brown to black may be observed. Mid to late season aboveground symptoms include light brown to grey superficial lesions in the stem. Cross-sections of the lower stem and taproot may become streaked with gray hyphae and microsclerotia, giving a marbled appearance

diagnostic_features.value: Presence of microsclerotia in vascular tissue, pith, and mature dry pods; marbled appearance of cross-sections of lower stem and taproot with gray hyphae and microsclerotia; small black spots (pycnidia) irregularly dispersed across stem surface; tiny black specks or dots resembling charcoal dust on or just inside the tissue surface.
diagnostic_features.quote: A characteristic sign of the pathogen on soybean is the presence of microsclerotia in the vascular tissue, in the pith, and mature and dry pods. Cross-sections of the lower stem and taproot may become streaked with gray hyphae and microsclerotia, giving a marbled appearance. On plant stems, small black spots (pycnidia) can be seen irregularly dispersed across the surface.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: The causal agent of this vulnerable fungal disease is Cercospora sojina K. hara.

type_of_disease.quote: The causal agent of this vulnerable fungal disease is Cercospora sojina K. hara.

affected_parts.quote: Symptoms of frogeye leaf spot are most visible and typically seen on leaves, but can also occur on stems, pods, and seeds.

summary.value: Early symptoms are small, dark, water-soaked circular to angular lesions (generally 1-5 mm diameter) that expand into brown to grayish spots with brown-reddish borders. A yellow halo may be present around leaf spots. Centers of spots may show small black dots (spores) or fall away leaving a 'shot hole' appearance.
summary.quote: Early FLS symptoms are small, dark, water soaked, circular to angular lesion (generally 1-5 mm diameter). As the disease progresses, the lesions expand and becomes brown to grayish with a brown-reddish border. A yellow halo may be observed around leaf spots, but are not necessarily present on all FLS lesions.

diagnostic_features.value: The reddish-brown or purple ring surrounding round leaf spots distinguishes frogeye leaf spot. Small black dots resembling fine ground pepper (fungal spores) visible in the middle of lesions.
diagnostic_features.quote: Frogeye leaf spot can be distinguished from other soybean foliar diseases by the reddish-brown or purple ring surrounding the round leaf spots.

conflicts.note: NC State does not explicitly list seed as an affected part; UMN Extension includes seeds.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Infection by the fungus Diaporthe sojae can occur early in the growing season

type_of_disease.quote: Infection by the fungus Diaporthe sojae

affected_parts.quote: A characteristic symptom of D. sojae infection is parallel rows of black, flask-shaped specks or pycnidia on mature soybean stems or other dead/dying tissues (Figure 1). The pycnidia may also develop on dry, poorly developed pods

summary.value: Parallel rows of black, flask-shaped specks or pycnidia on mature soybean stems occurring later in the season (R6 to R8 growth stages). Pycnidia may also develop on dry, poorly developed pods, but may be dispersed randomly rather than arranged linearly.
summary.quote: A characteristic symptom of D. sojae infection is parallel rows of black, flask-shaped specks or pycnidia on mature soybean stems or other dead/dying tissues (Figure 1). The pycnidia may also develop on dry, poorly developed pods, but may be dispersed randomly rather than arranged linearly.

diagnostic_features.value: Parallel rows of black, flask-shaped pycnidia arranged linearly on stems; random dispersal on pods.
diagnostic_features.quote: A characteristic symptom of D. sojae infection is parallel rows of black, flask-shaped specks or pycnidia on mature soybean stems

conflicts.note: NC State refers to the disease caused by Diaporthe sojae (syn. P. phaseoli) as 'Pod Blight'; Bayer uses 'Pod and Stem Blight' for the same pathogen.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: The seed decay is caused primarily by the related fungus Phomopsis longicola or other species.

type_of_disease.quote: The seed decay is caused primarily by the related fungus Phomopsis longicola

affected_parts.quote: Infected seed are cracked, shriveled, dull, and may have a gray mold on them.

summary.value: Infected seed are cracked, shriveled, dull, and may have a gray mold on them.
summary.quote: Infected seed are cracked, shriveled, dull, and may have a gray mold on them.

diagnostic_features.value: Seed infected by pod and stem blight may decompose after harvest and have low viability; seedlings grown from infected seeds may often be blighted.
diagnostic_features.quote: Seed infected by pod and stem blight may decompose after harvest and have low viability. Seedlings grown from infected seeds may often be blighted.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Phyllosticta leaf spot is caused by the fungus Phyllosticta sojicola

type_of_disease.quote: Phyllosticta leaf spot is caused by the fungus Phyllosticta sojicola

affected_parts.quote: Phyllosticta leaf spot is an uncommon foliar disease

summary.value: Lesions most often occur on leaves and are circular, oval, and irregular or V-shaped. Lesions appear gray or tan and have a narrow, dark margin. Irregularly shaped tan/brownish lesions with purplish margins may be observed in the lower canopy.
summary.quote: Lesions most often occur on leaves and are circular, oval, and irregular or V-shaped. Lesions appear gray or tan and have a narrow, dark margin.

diagnostic_features.value: In older lesions, numerous small, black specks (i.e., pycnidia) may be visible.
diagnostic_features.quote: In older lesions, numerous small, black specks (i.e., pycnidia) may be visible.

conflicts.canonical_value: Lesions most often occur on leaves and are circular, oval, and irregular or V-shaped. Lesions appear gray or tan and have a narrow, dark margin.
conflicts.alternative_value: Irregularly shaped tan/brownish lesions with purplish margins in the lower canopy.
conflicts.note: CPN describes gray or tan lesions with narrow dark margin; Cornell CALS describes tan/brownish lesions with purplish margins. Both descriptions may reflect variation by lesion age or cultivar.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: The pathogen that causes Phytophthora damping-off, root, and stem rot of soybean is Phytophthora sojae.

type_of_disease.quote: Phytophthora sojae is a fungal-like pathogen

affected_parts.quote: brown lesions form on the roots, the roots rot and degrade, and a dark chocolate-brown discoloration of the stem often extends from below the soil line upward into lower parts of the plant. Leaves turn yellow, wilt

summary.value: Young plants show rapid yellowing and wilting with soft rot and collapse of the root. Mature plants exhibit general yellowing of lower leaves progressing upward, followed by wilting and death, with brown discolored roots and a dark chocolate-brown stem discoloration extending from below the soil line upward several nodes; leaves typically stay attached after plant death.
summary.quote: Symptoms in young plants include rapid yellowing and wilting accompanied by a soft rot and collapse of the root. More mature plants generally show reduced vigor and may be gradually killed as the growing season progresses. Foliar symptoms on older plants occur as general yellowing of the lower leaves that progresses upward on the plant, followed by wilting and death. The root system is usually severely affected such that lateral and branch roots are almost completely discolored. Tap roots show a brown discoloration on the surface and, if split, the inner tissues show a tan to brown discoloration. Perhaps the best diagnostic symptom of the disease on susceptible varieties is a lower stem discoloration that may extend several nodes up the stem.

diagnostic_features.value: The best diagnostic symptom on susceptible varieties is a lower stem discoloration (dark chocolate-brown) that may extend several nodes up the stem. Root system shows lateral and branch roots almost completely discolored; tap roots with brown surface discoloration and tan to brown inner tissue discoloration. Leaves turn yellow, wilt, and typically stay attached after plant death.
diagnostic_features.quote: Perhaps the best diagnostic symptom of the disease on susceptible varieties is a lower stem discoloration that may extend several nodes up the stem. The root system is usually severely affected such that lateral and branch roots are almost completely discolored. Tap roots show a brown discoloration on the surface and, if split, the inner tissues show a tan to brown discoloration.

look_alikes.quote: This disease can be confused with stem canker, which usually starts at a node and spreads up and down the stems of infected plants... It is important to recognize that Pythium is a related pathogen that causes similar damage and symptoms on seeds and seedlings.

conflicts.note: OSU Ohioline titles the disease 'Phytophthora Damping-off and Root Rot' while UMN Extension uses 'Phytophthora root and stem rot'; both refer to the same pathogen Phytophthora sojae causing the same disease complex.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Powdery mildew of soybean is caused by the fungus Erysiphe diffusa (syn. Microsphaera diffusa)

type_of_disease.quote: Powdery mildew of soybean is caused by the fungus Erysiphe diffusa

affected_parts.quote: Symptoms include a white, powdery coating on infected leaves. White to gray powdery patches begin small, but patches coalesce to cover the entire leaf as the disease progresses... Pods may become heavily infected and reduce pod fill resulting in shriveled, underdeveloped seed.

summary.value: White to gray powdery patches on leaves that begin small but coalesce to cover the entire leaf as disease progresses. Some varieties exhibit leaf yellowing, scorching, or rust-colored patch symptoms. Pods may become heavily infected resulting in shriveled, underdeveloped seed.
summary.quote: Symptoms include a white, powdery coating on infected leaves. White to gray powdery patches begin small, but patches coalesce to cover the entire leaf as the disease progresses. Severity of symptoms may vary amongst cultivars. Some varieties exhibit leaf yellowing, scorching, or rust-colored patch symptoms.

diagnostic_features.value: White, powdery coating on infected leaves that coalesces to cover the entire leaf; necrotic tissues may mimic herbicide injury symptoms.
diagnostic_features.quote: Symptoms include a white, powdery coating on infected leaves. White to gray powdery patches begin small, but patches coalesce to cover the entire leaf as the disease progresses... Necrotic tissues may mimic symptoms of herbicide injuries.

look_alikes.quote: Necrotic tissues may mimic symptoms of herbicide injuries.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Northern ( Diaporthe caulivora )

type_of_disease.quote: Northern stem canker is caused by the fungus Diaporthe phaseolorum var. caulivora

affected_parts.quote: reddish-brown lesions that appear at the base of branches or leaf petioles. These small lesions can develop into elongated, sunken, dark brown cankers that spread up and down the stem... Plant parts above the lesions may die... pods can abort. Leaves may develop necrosis and chlorosis

summary.value: Early symptoms are reddish-brown lesions at the base of branches or leaf petioles that develop into elongated, sunken, dark brown cankers spreading up and down the stem. Tiny black dots called perithecia may appear on the stem singly or in clustered groups on plants killed by stem canker. Leaves may develop necrosis and chlorosis between the veins.
summary.quote: Early symptoms include reddish-brown lesions that appear at the base of branches or leaf petioles. These small lesions can develop into elongated, sunken, dark brown cankers that spread up and down the stem (Figures 5 and 6). Tiny black dots called perithecia (spore producing fungal structures) may appear on the stem singly or in clustered groups on plants killed by stem canker... Leaves may also develop necrosis and chlorosis between the veins and may remain attached after death.

diagnostic_features.value: Elongated, sunken, dark brown cankers on stems with tiny black perithecia. Reddish-brown discoloration may also occur inside the stem. Lesions often develop at and remain darker at nodes. Stem cankers do not impact the root, unlike Phytophthora root rot.
diagnostic_features.quote: Cankers can also look similar to the lesions produced by Phytophthora root rot. However, Phytophthora root rot will also cause root rot with a continuous lesion that extends from root through the stem, while stem cankers do not impact the root.

look_alikes.quote: Cankers can also look similar to the lesions produced by Phytophthora root rot... Northern ( Diaporthe caulivora ) and southern stem canker ( Diaporthe aspalathi ) can be found throughout US soybean growing areas. Both diseases have similar symptomology.

conflicts.note: UMN Extension uses the older varietal epithet Diaporthe phaseolorum var. caulivora; Bayer uses the current species name Diaporthe caulivora.

type_of_disease.quote: In most cases, it can be attributed to an imbalance in the source-sink relationship within the plant

affected_parts.quote: Most commonly, this is seen in the stems, leaves or pods but can also occur when petioles and leaves remain attached to the stem

summary.value: All or part of the soybean plant remains green while the rest of the plant or neighboring plants mature, most commonly seen in stems, leaves or pods; stems remain moist while pods and seeds have ripened.
summary.quote: the condition occurs when all or part of the soybean plant remains green, while the rest of the plant or neighboring plants senesce (mature). Most commonly, this is seen in the stems, leaves or pods but can also occur when petioles and leaves remain attached to the stem, resulting in green leaves remaining on the plant when plants would normally mature

diagnostic_features.value: Stems and occasionally leaves remain green and moist after pods and seeds have ripened and turned brown; excessive leaves on plant and green stems when neighboring plants are near harvest maturity.
diagnostic_features.quote: Stems of plants remain green after the pods and seeds have ripened and are brown and ready for harvest. Occasionally the stems and leaves remain green after the pods have matured, which is well past the time when the whole plant is normally brown and dry.

conflicts.note: UMN Extension lists stems and sometimes leaves; OSU Extension additionally lists pods

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Fusarium virgulifome (previously named Fusaium solani f.sp. glycines).

type_of_disease.quote: This is a soilborne fungus that appears to primarily infect soybean

affected_parts.quote: SDS is primarily a root disease but typically also affects leaves and causes defoliation. Brown to grey discolored areas develop in the vascular tissue of the lower stem

summary.value: Leaf symptoms begin as scattered yellow diffuse spots between veins that expand to become brown lesions surrounded by chlorotic areas; leaves may be cupped or curled. Brown to grey discolored areas develop in the vascular tissue of the lower stem. Roots may show surface blue fungal growth in moist conditions.
summary.quote: Leaf symptoms often begin as scattered yellow, diffuses pots between veins. The spots typically expand between veins to become brown lesions surrounded by chlorotic areas, and the leaves may be cupped or curled. Brown to grey discolored areas develop in the vascular tissue of the lower stem, and can typically be seen by removing the epidermis of the stem of fresh plants. SDS also causes root rot, and roots may have surface blue fungal growth in moist conditions.

diagnostic_features.value: The pith remains white, which distinguishes SDS from brown stem rot.
diagnostic_features.quote: The pith remains white, which is a diagnostic feature that distinguishes SDS from brown stem rot (BSR).

look_alikes.quote: The pith remains white, which is a diagnostic feature that distinguishes SDS from brown stem rot (BSR).

conflicts.note: UMN notes the pathogen was previously named Fusarium solani f.sp. glycines; current accepted name is Fusarium virguliforme

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: The species most frequently associated with root rot on soybean are F. solani and F. oxysporum

type_of_disease.quote: Fusarium oxysporum is an ascomycete fungus found commonly in the soil.

affected_parts.quote: Root rot appears as reddish-brown to dark brown discolored roots and poor nodulation. Foliar symptoms of Fusarium wilt include scorching of the upper leaves, while middle and lower canopy leaves can turn chlorotic and later wither and drop from the plant. Infected plants have brown vascular tissue in the roots and stems and show wilting of the stem tips.

summary.value: Root rot appears as reddish-brown to dark brown discolored roots with poor nodulation and cortical decay or vascular discoloration. Foliar symptoms include interveinal chlorosis, scorching of upper leaves, wilting, and defoliation. Infected plants have brown vascular tissue in roots and stems.
summary.quote: Root rot appears as reddish-brown to dark brown discolored roots and poor nodulation. Foliar symptoms of Fusarium wilt include scorching of the upper leaves, while middle and lower canopy leaves can turn chlorotic and later wither and drop from the plant. Infected plants have brown vascular tissue in the roots and stems and show wilting of the stem tips.

diagnostic_features.value: Brown vascular tissue in roots and stems with wilting of stem tips; no external decay or stem lesions above the soil line. Reddish to brown vascular discoloration extending into the lower stem. Secondary roots may develop above decomposed lateral roots on the upper taproot.
diagnostic_features.quote: Infected plants have brown vascular tissue in the roots and stems and show wilting of the stem tips. External decay or stem lesions are not seen above the soil line.

look_alikes.quote: Fusarium species are often isolated from soybean roots that are also infected by other pathogens (e.g. Pythium, Phytophthora, and Rhizoctonia)

conflicts.note: NC State source focuses on wilt aspect; UMN source focuses on root rot; CPN source combines both as 'Fusarium Root Rot and Wilt'; ISU index lists as 'Fusarium Wilt and Root Rot'

affected_parts.quote: white mold is often recognized by fluffy, white growth on soybean stems. Initial symptoms generally develop from R3 to R6 as gray to white lesions at the nodes... summary.value: White mold is recognized by fluffy, white growth on soybean stems with gray to white lesions at nodes that rapidly progress and girdle stems. Lesions expand and plant tops become grayish-green, then wilt and die. Dead leaves remain attached to stems while turning brown, and characteristic black sclerotia are visible embedded within white mold on stem lesions. Dry dead stems develop a bleached white appearance.
summary.quote: white mold is often recognized by fluffy, white growth on soybean stems. Initial symptoms generally develop from R3 to R6 as gray to white lesions at the nodes. Characteristic black sclerotia eventually are visible and embedded within mold on stem lesions

diagnostic_features.value: Characteristic black sclerotia embedded within white fluffy mold on stems and inside stems as the plant approaches death; dead leaves remaining attached to stems while turning completely brown; white cottony seeds in pods.
diagnostic_features.quote: Characteristic black sclerotia eventually are visible and embedded within mold on stem lesions, and inside the stem as the plant approaches death.
